source.title: Deep Causal Transcoding: A Framework for Mechanistically Eliciting Latent Behaviors in Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study directly investigates whether harmful-request jailbreak behavior is represented by one direction or multiple directions, and reports interventions that refine the single-primary-direction account.
record.gate_note: The author discusses the original difference-in-means refusal direction and cites its results, but those cited results are not this study's results. The study's own relevant experiments use DCT-learned features and a Sure-versus-Sorry logit score, not direct refusal rates. The 32B and capability-elicitation demonstrations do not test the listed refusal-direction versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses its own DCT steering and ablation experiments on Qwen1.5-7B-Chat, scored by a Sure-minus-Sorry logit proxy for refusal. It argues against a pure single-direction account and proposes one primary direction (ablation) plus many secondary directions (addition). That bears on V4's 'dominant direction plus others'. It does not use the difference-in-means direction, so V1 is not directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author finds >200 linearly independent 'harmless' directions that elicit jailbreaks when added, and that averaging does not beat the best one. Ablating an averaged direction works better than ablating any individual feature. The author proposes one primary harmful direction used in-distribution for refusal, plus many secondary directions usable via addition. The author argues that safety training targeting a single direction (e.g., circuit breakers) may leave models vulnerable, and calls the multiplicity question not conclusively settled.
record.recipe_differences: Uses deep causal transcoding to learn steering features from downstream activation changes, then adds or directionally ablates those features. It does not use the original harmful-versus-harmless difference-in-means direction or its all-layer, all-position weight projection.
record.method_sensitivity: Source-layer versus target-layer features produce different ablation scores; individual versus averaged features produce different scores. The source-layer additions are evaluated using the top 240 features selected at a jailbreak-score threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: DCT latent steering jailbreaks circuit-breaker (representation-rerouted) Mistral-7B-Instruct-v2 at 62% ASR (HarmBench classifier), versus 6.2% reported by Zou et al.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised latent steering directions can bypass representation-rerouting safety training; this does not show suppression of the difference-in-means refusal direction.

record.problems: The refusal-related experiments use a Sure-versus-Sorry logit difference as a jailbreak proxy, not direct refusal rates. The tables report no uncertainty estimates; the multiplicity evidence is from one reported feature set and includes subjective judgments of elicited behavior. The study does not test preservation of general capability under refusal-direction removal.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant table or text results omitted.

untested.parts: Difference-in-means direction, its ablation and addition, refusal rates, and capability preservation are all untested. Only DCT features with a logit proxy are used.
No affine or cone geometry is fitted. Refusal rates are not measured. Results come from one DCT run on one model, with no uncertainty.
There is no test of whether attacks suppress the refusal direction. Circuit-breaker jailbreaking is not training against ablation.
The 32B and Mistral runs are qualitative or separate attacks, not a transfer test.

missing.what: Author's comment reports output-direction (u) multiplicity for the same top 240 features: mean |cos| .25, condition number 27. Output directions are thus no more collinear than input ones.
missing.locator: Comments, Andrew Mack reply to Jacob G-W

missing.what: Qualitative report that Qwen1.5-32B-Chat DCT (layers 10→20) also yields many 'helpful-only' jailbreak features. No numbers are given.
missing.locator: Deeper models: constant depth horizon suffices

record.verdict_notes: All refusal evidence uses a Sure-minus-Sorry logit score with no unsteered baseline and no error bars, from a single DCT run (first shuffle, n=8). The author explicitly reconciles these results with Arditi et al. rather than refuting them. Informal Alignment Forum post, not peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not find or ablate the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, remove it from every layer and position, test adding it to induce refusals on harmless requests, or assess whether general capabilities are preserved.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration experiment is reported.
The study does not test whether attacks suppress the original refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The study does not establish a general affine or cone geometry; its multiplicity evidence is from DCT features and jailbreak-score proxies on the tested settings.
No separate harmfulness judgment and refusal-decision representations are tested.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or systematic model-variant transfer test of the refusal direction is reported.
The study does not vary safety-training data or timing to test how training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.

relation.reason: Runs its own steering and directional-ablation experiments and explicitly sets the results against Arditi et al.'s single direction.

tranche.reason: Its own addition and ablation results on Qwen1.5-7B-Chat argue that a single-direction account needs restating as one primary direction plus many secondary ones. Caveat: the outcome is a Sure-minus-Sorry logit proxy with no refusal rate.

source_check.notes: The pack lists the verdicts without [lN] ids, so I numbered them l1–l3 in order. Every result is a Sure-minus-Sorry logit proxy from one DCT run (first shuffle, n=8, test on 100 AdvBench prompts), with no unsteered baseline and no uncertainty for Tables 3–5. 'uncertainty=y' on the call applies only to Figure 1. In a comment reply the author adds geometry for the u-features (|dot| .25, condition number 27), which no row records.

statements.correction: DCT: no uncertainty for r1–r9; sd .19 is spread of pairwise |dot|; only Figure 1 (a separate sample-complexity experiment, 10 shuffles) has error bars. Addition: best individual 14.19 > vavg 9.80, ±vsvd 10.31. Author's framing: one primary direction (ablation), many secondary directions that jailbreak via addition.
statements.problem: All DCT numbers are correct. But the 'why' says DCT reports uncertainty, and none is given for the cited results (Tables 3–4, the 240 count, the geometry). The headline 'weaker others' does not fit DCT's addition results, where the best single feature beats the aggregates. And DCT's additions are causal tests of extra directions too, not only its ablations.

statements.correction: Author attributes the lower target-layer scores to u-features capturing downstream effects of the 'should refuse' direction rather than the direction itself.
statements.problem: DCT figures and the 'same pattern but much weaker' reading are correct. Nuance: 'layer' here means where the DCT features were learned (output factors u at layer 20 vs input factors v at layer 10). The text does not state the ablation site. The author reads Table 5 as corroborating the primary/secondary view.

statements.correction: The post also adds DCT features on Qwen1.5-32B-Chat, but only qualitatively and toward compliance. No refusal induction above 10B, so the untested point stands.
statements.problem: Correct for this study: r1–r3 add features or their aggregates toward compliance (jailbreak), not refusal, on a 7B model.

statements.correction: Logit score is the outcome for r1–r3 and r7–r12; r4 is a threshold count (5.0, called arbitrary); r5–r6 are |dot| and condition number.
statements.problem: Correct that DCT's outcome is a Sure-minus-Sorry final-logit difference, not a refusal rate. Minor: r4–r6 are a count and geometry measures on features selected by that score, not logit scores themselves.
